title: Drainage Systems and Rivers of India and Andhra Pradesh
intake_rule: Each printed page is read once from its rendered image. Facts, concepts, maps, tables and printed PYQs are recorded before notes or MCQs are authored. Handwritten annotations are ignored.
table_policy: Printed tables are preserved cell-by-cell, then corrected, dated and enriched. Concept explanations use paragraphs; comparisons and datasets remain responsive semantic tables.

pages.heading: Drainage system fundamentals

facts.claim: Runoff begins in small rills and rivulets, may enlarge into gullies and streams, and joins to form a river.
A river channel is the route through which river water flows; the river mouth is the place where the river enters a sea, lake or another river.
A tributary joins a main river, whereas a distributary branches away from the main channel, commonly near a delta or lower course.
A river system consists of the main river and its connected tributaries and distributaries.
The printed map depicts major Indian river systems, state boundaries and drainage directions; map labels must be checked against current political names and correct river courses.

pages.heading: Catchment, basin, watershed and river-origin classifications

facts.claim: A river catchment is the land area from which runoff drains to a specified river or point; a watershed is also used for a drainage area but scale and disciplinary usage vary.
A drainage basin is the entire area drained by a river and its tributaries.
A drainage divide or water divide is the elevated boundary separating adjacent drainage basins; the interfluve is the land between neighbouring streams.
Antecedent rivers established their courses before major uplift and maintained them by incision; Indus, Sutlej and Brahmaputra are standard Himalayan examples.
The book calls antecedent rivers 'superimposed' in the same sentence, but antecedent and superimposed drainage are distinct concepts and must not be treated as synonyms.
facts.verification_note: Explain antecedence and superimposition separately with landform history.

facts.claim: The Trans-Himalayan river group includes the Indus, Brahmaputra and Sutlej systems; other printed names require spelling and basin verification.
Many Peninsular rivers are consequent rivers following the regional slope, while rejuvenation refers to renewed erosional energy after uplift or base-level change; the two terms are not synonyms.
facts.verification_note: The printed line uses Consequent/Rejuvenated as if interchangeable; correct this in notes and MCQs.

pages.heading: Barak, Feni and the Godavari system

facts.claim: The Barak rises in the Manipur hills, flows through southern Assam and enters Bangladesh, where its branches form part of the Surma-Meghna system; the 2022 Kushiyara water agreement is time-sensitive current affairs.
The Feni is a transboundary river between India and Bangladesh in the Tripura-Chattogram region; current water-sharing and border-use statements require treaty-level verification.

Most large Peninsular rivers flow east toward the Bay of Bengal, while Narmada and Tapi are prominent west-flowing exceptions; Damodar, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Pennar and Kaveri are key east-flowing systems.
The Godavari rises near Trimbakeshwar in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra and flows east across the Deccan toward the Bay of Bengal; its commonly quoted length is about 1,465 km.
The Godavari drains parts of Maharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and smaller adjoining areas; exact state-wise basin shares require a dated official basin report.
In the lower delta the Godavari divides into distributary branches including Gautami, Vasishta and related channels; branch names and bifurcation order should follow an official delta map.

pages.heading: Godavari basin, tributaries and river towns

facts.claim: The Godavari has the largest basin among Peninsular rivers and is commonly called Dakshin Ganga or Vridha Ganga; printed basin area and state-percentage figures require an official dated source.
Major Godavari tributary systems include Pravara, Manjira, Maner, Pranahita, Indravati and Sabari; the Pranahita itself integrates the Wardha-Wainganga system.
The printed five lower-Godavari distributary names and their district routes must be preserved in a table but verified against a current delta and district map.

The printed pilgrimage-town list places Nashik, Trimbakeshwar, Nanded, Basar, Dharmapuri, Kaleshwaram, Bhadrachalam, Rajamahendravaram, Antarvedi and other sites along the Godavari system; town-river and current district relationships require row-level verification.
Godavari tributaries should be organised by left/right bank using downstream orientation rather than copied as a single list; printed bank assignments need individual confirmation.

pages.heading: Godavari tributaries and projects

facts.claim: Right-bank or southern tributaries described on the page include Darna, Pravara, Sindphana, Manjira, Maner and Kinnerasani; each origin, course and confluence must be verified individually.
Left-bank or northern tributary systems described include Kadam/Kaddam, Shivna, Purna, Pranahita, Indravati and Sabari; printed district names reflect older administrative maps in places.
Pranahita is a major Godavari tributary formed by the Wardha-Wainganga system and carries runoff from a large central Indian basin.
Indravati rises in the eastern uplands and flows through Chhattisgarh-Odisha-border landscapes before joining the Godavari; exact source and district path require current map verification.
Sabari and Sileru are linked to the lower Godavari system; hydropower projects and interstate water allocation on Sileru are infrastructure and policy facts that require current official sources.
The page lists multiple Godavari projects and interstate arrangements; project capacity, allocation and status must be separated from stable river-course facts.

pages.heading: Krishna basin profile

facts.claim: The Krishna rises near Mahabaleshwar in the Western Ghats and flows east through Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh to the Bay of Bengal; its commonly quoted length is about 1,400 km.
The Krishna is the second-largest east-flowing Peninsular river by basin after the Godavari; printed state-wise basin shares and exact area require a dated official basin source.
Major Krishna tributaries include Bhima, Tungabhadra, Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, Koyna, Musi, Dindi and other regional rivers; bank-side classification must use downstream orientation.
Tungabhadra is formed by the Tunga and Bhadra headstreams in Karnataka and is a major tributary of the Krishna.
The Krishna basin map shows tributaries, reservoirs and state boundaries schematically; project labels and district boundaries require current verification.

tables: IA03-T15 Krishna tributaries by bank

pages.heading: Krishna tributary detail

facts.claim: Koyna, Varna, Panchganga, Dudhaganga, Ghataprabha and Malaprabha are western or upper-basin tributaries of the Krishna system; origin districts and confluences require current administrative mapping.
The Tungabhadra is created by the confluence of Tunga and Bhadra and later joins the Krishna; its major tributaries include Varada and Hagari/Vedavati among others.

Bhima is a major Krishna tributary rising in the Western Ghats region and flowing through Maharashtra-Karnataka; the printed statement about its Telangana route requires correction against an official basin map.
Dindi and Halia are smaller tributary systems in the Telangana-Krishna basin context; local origin and confluence claims require basin-level verification.
The printed Krishna tributary list mixes rivers, sub-tributaries and district references; notes must reconstruct a hierarchy rather than reproduce a flat list.

pages.heading: Yamuna and major tributaries of the Ganga

facts.claim: The Yamuna rises from the Yamunotri glacier region, flows past the Delhi-Agra corridor and joins the Ganga at Prayagraj; exact source elevation and length require an official series.
The Yamuna is commonly described as the longest tributary of the Ganga in India; its major tributaries include Chambal, Sind, Betwa and Ken from the Peninsular side.
The Chambal rises near the Mhow/Janapav highland region, flows through Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, and joins the Yamuna in Uttar Pradesh; it is noted for ravines and badland topography.
Banas is a major tributary of the Chambal; Kali Sindh, Parbati and Shipra belong to the wider Chambal-Malwa drainage context but their exact confluence relationships must not be merged.
Sind, Betwa and Ken are right-bank tributaries of the Yamuna rising in the Peninsular uplands; printed origin points and lengths require one official basin source.

Tons/Tamas, Son and Damodar are important Ganga-system rivers from the Peninsular or plateau margin, but the printed wording sometimes mixes direct Ganga tributaries with tributaries of tributaries and must be organised hierarchically.
The highlighted 2024 Ujjain Vedic-clock statement is current-affairs material unrelated to river-system structure; it should be kept separate and verified independently if retained.

tables: IA03-T06 Yamuna tributaries and origin-course notes

pages.heading: Northern tributaries of the Ganga and introduction to the Indus

facts.claim: Ramganga, Gomti, Ghaghara, Gandak, Burhi Gandak, Kosi and Mahananda are important northern or left-bank tributaries of the Ganga system, but each river's immediate receiving channel must be checked individually.
The Gomti rises in the Pilibhit region and joins the Ganga near the Ghazipur area; Lucknow and Jaunpur lie along its course.

The Ghaghara/Karnali system rises in the trans-Himalayan-Tibetan region, flows through Nepal and joins the Ganga in Bihar; Sarayu/Sharda naming must be handled carefully because regional usage differs by reach.
The Gandak/Narayani and Kosi systems descend from Nepal to the Bihar plain; the Kosi has shifted channels and built a large alluvial fan, contributing to recurrent flooding.
The printed claim that Kosi rises from seven named streams and is called Saptakosi should be presented as a tributary-system convention, with individual names and transboundary spelling verified.
The Mahananda is a northern tributary reaching the Ganga-Padma system after flowing through the Darjeeling foothill and north Bengal-Bihar region.

The Indus rises in the Tibetan plateau region near the Kailash-Manasarovar area, flows through Ladakh and then Pakistan to the Arabian Sea; the printed source place and elevation require an authoritative transboundary source.

tables: IA03-T07 Ganga left-bank tributaries by origin, course and confluence

pages.heading: Indus basin, tributaries and Punjab rivers

facts.claim: The Indus crosses Ladakh and the western Himalayan region before flowing through Pakistan to the Arabian Sea; printed total length and basin-area values differ by international and national segment definitions.
Tarbela Dam is on the Indus in Pakistan; dam dimensions and superlatives require a current official source.

Important upper and western Indus tributaries include Shyok, Nubra, Gilgit, Zanskar, Kabul, Kurram and Gomal; the printed bank-side grouping must follow the direction of the main Indus channel and should be verified carefully.
Jhelum rises at Verinag in Kashmir, flows through Wular Lake and joins the Chenab system in Pakistan; the page's reservoir and project references need present-name verification.
Chenab is formed by the Chandra and Bhaga headstreams in Himachal Pradesh and then flows through Jammu and Kashmir into Pakistan.

Ravi rises in the Himachal Himalaya, Beas rises near Rohtang, and Sutlej rises in the Tibetan region and enters India through Himachal Pradesh; printed lengths and source elevations require a single official dataset.
The printed map depicts the Indus and Punjab river network, including Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej; map labels and international boundaries must be read as schematic.

pages.heading: Sutlej, Punjab doabs and Brahmaputra profile

facts.claim: The Sutlej enters India through Himachal Pradesh, is joined by the Beas in Punjab and continues into Pakistan as part of the Indus system; Bhakra-Nangal is a major project on the Sutlej system.
A doab is the land between two rivers; Sind Sagar, Chaj, Rachna, Bari and Bist/Jalandhar are the traditional Punjab doabs, each defined by a specific river pair.
The Brahmaputra rises in the Tibetan region and flows eastward there as the Yarlung Tsangpo before turning through the eastern syntaxis and entering Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang/Dihang system.
After receiving the Dibang and Lohit systems in Assam, the river is known as the Brahmaputra and flows westward through the Assam valley before turning south into Bangladesh as the Jamuna.
The printed Brahmaputra length and basin-area values use different territorial segments and require an authoritative source-year and definition before comparison.
Majuli is a Brahmaputra river island shaped by channel migration, erosion and deposition; area, population and 'largest river island' claims are date- and definition-sensitive.

tables: IA03-T09 Punjab doabs and bounding rivers

pages.heading: Brahmaputra tributaries and transboundary rivers

facts.claim: The printed table groups Brahmaputra tributaries by north/right bank and south/left bank, but bank designation must be determined while looking downstream and each tributary should be checked individually.

Subansiri, Kameng, Manas, Sankosh, Raidak, Jaldhaka and Torsa are among important northern tributary systems, while Dibang, Lohit, Burhi Dihing, Dhansiri, Kopili and related rivers enter from the south or eastern hills; printed lists require basin-by-basin verification.
The Teesta rises in the Sikkim Himalaya, flows through north Bengal and joins the Brahmaputra/Jamuna system in Bangladesh; it changed course substantially after the 1787 flood.

The book's statement that the Teesta formed a permanent boundary between India and Bangladesh requires correction: it is a transboundary river, but the international boundary is not simply the river's full course.
Dibang, Lohit and Burhi Dihing rise in the eastern Himalayan-Arunachal sector and join the Brahmaputra system; names and exact confluences must be mapped rather than treated as one channel.

The page lists projects and parks associated with Brahmaputra tributaries, including Subansiri and Manas; current project status and protected-area relationships are time-sensitive and require official verification.

tables: IA03-T10 Brahmaputra tributaries by bank

pages.heading: Himalayan and Peninsular rivers comparison; basin-size classification

facts.claim: The printed 12-row comparison contrasts Himalayan and Peninsular rivers by examples, water source, perennial or seasonal character, basin size, gradient, tributary structure, valley form, age, length and drainage pattern.
Major Himalayan examples include the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra systems; major Peninsular examples include Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi, Kaveri, Pennar, Narmada and Tapi.

Himalayan rivers receive snow/glacier melt and monsoon rainfall and are generally perennial, whereas many Peninsular rivers depend more strongly on seasonal rainfall; this is a dominant pattern with local exceptions.

Himalayan basins and tributary networks are generally larger, and the rivers often form deep gorges in mountains and broad meanders in plains; Peninsular rivers flow through older, more stable terrain and commonly occupy shallower, broader valleys.
Himalayan rivers commonly show dendritic drainage over broad plains, while Peninsular drainage includes dendritic, trellis, radial and other patterns depending on structure and relief.

The printed percentages assigning 77% of total drainage area to Himalayan rivers and 23% to Peninsular rivers require a clearly identified dataset and should not be scored without source verification.
facts.verification_note: Hold exact percentages until the original statistical source and category definitions are opened.

facts.claim: The book classifies Indian river basins by catchment size as major above 20,000 sq km, medium 2,000-20,000 sq km and minor below 2,000 sq km.
Printed counts and water-share percentages for major, medium and minor basins are dataset-sensitive and require an official dated source before scoring.

pages.heading: Basin-size statistics and introduction to the Ganga system

facts.claim: The page continues printed counts and water-share estimates for major, medium and minor basins; all numbers require the same dated official dataset and consistent basin threshold definitions.
The Ganga headstream Bhagirathi rises from the Gangotri glacier system near Gaumukh, while the Alaknanda system joins it at Devprayag, after which the river is called the Ganga.
The Ganga enters the plains near Haridwar and flows generally southeastward across the northern plains before entering Bangladesh, where its main distributary system is known as the Padma.

The printed map shows the Ganga and its major Himalayan and Peninsular tributaries, including Yamuna, Ramganga, Gomti, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi, Son and Damodar; map position and bank-side classification must be verified individually.
The book begins a length and basin-profile description of the Ganga; exact lengths by state and basin area must retain the source and measurement convention.

pages.heading: Lower Krishna tributaries, Mahanadi and Cauvery

facts.claim: Musi, Paleru and Munneru are tributaries associated with the Krishna system; their origins, district routes and confluence locations must be represented as separate river profiles rather than one combined list.

The Musi flows through Hyderabad and joins the Krishna in the present Nalgonda district region; the printed district description predates later administrative reorganisation and must be updated carefully.
The Mahanadi rises in the Sihawa highlands of present-day Chhattisgarh, flows through Chhattisgarh and Odisha, and reaches the Bay of Bengal through a deltaic system.

The book prints an approximate Mahanadi length of 858 km, basin area of about 142,000 sq km and basin shares of 53% in Chhattisgarh and 46% in Odisha; these figures require one dated official basin source before scoring.

Seonath, Hasdeo, Mand, Ib, Ong, Tel and Jonk are important tributaries of the Mahanadi, and the printed basin map additionally labels Pairi and Sondur; bank-side classification must be checked from an official basin map.
The Cauvery rises at Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri hills of Kodagu, flows through Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and enters the Bay of Bengal through a deltaic distributary network.

The book prints a Cauvery length of about 805 km, a basin area of 81,155 sq km and state shares of 55.8% Karnataka, 41% Tamil Nadu, 3% Kerala and 0.2% Puducherry; retain these only after verification against the current official basin profile.

Lakshman Tirtha, Kabini, Suvarnavathi, Bhavani, Amaravathi, Hemavathi, Harangi, Shimsha and Arkavathi are important Cauvery tributaries; the exact bank and confluence of each should be taught in a comparison table.

The Cauvery divides around Srirangam island and forms a major delta in Tamil Nadu; statements about its islands and distributaries require precise geographical wording rather than the printed superlative claim.

pages.heading: Penna and other east-flowing Peninsular rivers

facts.claim: The Penna rises in the Nandi Hills region of Karnataka, flows through Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, and enters the Bay of Bengal near the Nellore coast; modern district names and its exact outlet should be verified from official basin material.

The book prints a Penna length of about 600 km, a basin area of roughly 55,000 sq km and an Andhra Pradesh share of 87%; these figures and the phrase 'Rayalaseema lifeline' must be sourced before use in scored questions.

Chitravati, Papagni and Cheyyeru are listed as right-bank tributaries of the Penna, while Jayamangali, Kunderu and Sagileru are listed as left-bank tributaries; each bank classification must be checked against flow direction and an official basin map.
The Brahmani forms from the confluence of the Sankh and South Koel and flows through Odisha to the Bay of Bengal; the printed source wording and its stated length require official verification.
The Baitarani rises in the Kendujhar highlands of Odisha and flows eastward to the Bay of Bengal through the Odisha coastal system.

The Subarnarekha rises in the Chota Nagpur Plateau near Ranchi, flows through Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha, and reaches the Bay of Bengal; the printed length of 395 km requires official verification.

The Tamraparni rises in the Agasthyamalai sector of the Western Ghats in Tamil Nadu and reaches the Gulf of Mannar; it is also called Thamirabarani, but the printed claim that it alone is perennial in Tamil Nadu needs authoritative qualification.

The Palar, Ponnaiyar and Vaigai are additional east-flowing Peninsular rivers whose origins, state routes, lengths and outlets must be verified individually rather than memorised from the page's short entries.

pages.heading: Major west-flowing Peninsular rivers

facts.claim: The Narmada flows west through a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges, rises at Amarkantak and enters the Gulf of Khambhat through an estuarine mouth.

The book prints a Narmada length of 1,312 km, a basin area near 99,000 sq km and state shares of 97% Madhya Pradesh, 1.5% Gujarat and 1.5% Maharashtra; verify all values against the same official basin source.

The Narmada is associated with the Marble Rocks and Dhuandhar Falls near Jabalpur and has tributaries including Barna, Banjar, Hiran, Tawa, Kundi, Shakkar, Kolar and Orsang; names and bank positions require map verification.
The Tapi rises near Multai in Madhya Pradesh, flows west roughly parallel to the Narmada through Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat, and enters the Gulf of Khambhat near Surat.
The Mahi rises in Madhya Pradesh, crosses Rajasthan and Gujarat, and enters the Gulf of Khambhat; its printed length, basin area and state shares require official verification.
The Sabarmati rises in the Aravalli hills, flows through Rajasthan and Gujarat, and enters the Gulf of Khambhat; the name and role of the Dharoi project require separate verification.

The Bhadar is a west-flowing river of Gujarat entering the Arabian Sea, while the Luni is an inland-drainage river that rises near Ajmer and loses itself in the Rann of Kachchh region rather than reaching the open sea as a normal coastal river.
The page groups west-flowing rivers by course, basin, tributaries and outlet; these attributes should be consolidated into a comparison table for Narmada, Tapi, Mahi, Sabarmati, Bhadar and Luni.

pages.heading: Inland-drainage rivers and short west-coast rivers

facts.claim: The Luni rises near Pushkar in the Aravalli region, flows southwest across Rajasthan and Gujarat, and dissipates in the Rann of Kachchh; printed length and tributary lists require official basin verification.
The Banas mentioned here is an inland-drainage river of the Rajasthan desert sector and must not be confused with the Banas tributary of the Chambal.

The Ghaggar is a seasonal river associated with the Shivalik foothills and northwestern plains; claims about its ancient identity and disappearance require archaeological and hydrological qualification.

Short west-flowing rivers of Maharashtra listed on the page include Vaitarna, Savitri and Savitri-related coastal systems; each origin and outlet must be checked because the printed entries are brief and may conflate nearby rivers.

The Sharavathi of Karnataka is associated with Jog Falls, while the Kali, Netravati and Bedti are additional west-flowing Karnataka rivers; origin, projects and exact outlets should be presented in a corrected comparison table.
The printed coastal-river map labels Mandovi, Zuari, Kali, Sharavathi, Netravati, Bharathapuzha, Periyar and Pamba, illustrating the short, steep west-flowing drainage of the Western Ghats.

pages.heading: Goa and Kerala rivers; important waterfalls

facts.claim: The Zuari and Mandovi are major Goa river-estuary systems flowing to the Arabian Sea; the printed claim about the largest river and the historical name Gomati require reliable state or basin sources.

The Periyar is Kerala's longest river, rises in the Western Ghats and flows west to the Arabian Sea; Mullaperiyar lies on the Periyar system and the interstate water dispute requires neutral, current wording.
Bharathapuzha is an important west-flowing Kerala river, also called Nila; the page's rank and length statements require confirmation from Kerala government data.

The Pamba flows through Kerala and is closely associated with Sabarimala; its origin, basin relationships and nickname 'Dakshina Bhagirathi' should be distinguished from exam-oriented traditional usage.

The printed waterfall table gives Kunchikal on the Varahi in Karnataka, Barehipani in Odisha and Nohkalikai in Meghalaya, with their printed heights and waterfall types; every cell requires verification because waterfall height and type vary by measurement convention.

The page separately claims Chitrakote is India's widest waterfall, Victoria Falls the world's widest, Angel Falls the world's highest, Niagara the world's largest, Talakona Andhra Pradesh's highest and Kuntala Telangana's highest; these superlatives must remain unscored until a defined metric and authoritative source are established.

pages.heading: Major Indian lakes and reservoirs by state

facts.claim: Limnology is the scientific study of inland waters, including lakes; potamology specifically concerns rivers. The terms must be explained rather than treated as interchangeable labels.
The Jammu and Kashmir group printed on the page includes Wular, Dal, Pangong, Manasbal and Surinsar-Mansar; their freshwater, saline, brackish or transboundary status must be stated individually.

Pangong Tso is a high-altitude transboundary endorheic lake extending across India and China; the printed 40:50:10 territorial split is politically and cartographically sensitive and must not be scored without a current authoritative source.

The Himachal Pradesh list includes Renuka, Suraj Tal, Khajjiar and other highland lakes, while Sikkim includes Tsomgo; all printed elevation and superlative claims require official state or wetland-source verification.
Surajkund in Haryana is a historic artificial reservoir; the name should not be confused with Suraj Tal, a natural high-altitude lake in Himachal Pradesh.
Rajasthan's printed lake list includes Sambhar, Didwana, Degana, Tal Chhapar, Dhebar or Jaisamand, Rajsamand, Nakki and Pushkar; saline, freshwater and artificial-lake categories must be separated.
Jaisamand, also called Dhebar Lake, is an artificial lake in Rajasthan; the page's rank, dimensions, catchment and project-era figures must be verified against Rajasthan government records.
Nal Sarovar in Gujarat, Nainital and Bhimtal in Uttarakhand, and Lonar in Maharashtra represent different lake origins and environments; Lonar is an impact-crater lake in basaltic terrain.
Kerala's Ashtamudi and Vembanad are backwater or lagoon-estuary systems; printed claims about the country's longest lake and largest spit lake require definition-based verification.

Kolleru is a freshwater lake between the Krishna and Godavari delta regions and is a Ramsar wetland; its area varies seasonally and by notified boundary, so the printed 245 sq km must be contextualised.

Pulicat is a brackish-water lagoon shared by Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu; printed total area and 96:4 state-share figures require verification, and its national rank depends on the definition of lagoon size.

Chilika is a large brackish-water coastal lagoon in Odisha and an internationally important Ramsar wetland; its surface area changes seasonally, so the printed 900-1,165 sq km range must be tied to a dated source.

pages.heading: Lake continuation and river lengths with riverbank cities

facts.claim: The page continues Chilika and lists Gurudongmar, Bhimtal and Naini among notable Himalayan lakes and Loktak in Manipur; Loktak is known for floating phumdis and Keibul Lamjao National Park.

The printed table compares river length and selected riverbank cities for the Brahmaputra, Indus, Ganga, Godavari, Krishna, Yamuna, Narmada, Sutlej, Chambal, Mahanadi, Cauvery, Chenab, Son, Kosi, Jhelum, Tapi, Ramganga, Mahi and Sabarmati; every row must be preserved and checked against a consistent length convention.

The table distinguishes total international length from length within India for transboundary rivers such as the Brahmaputra, Indus, Sutlej and Chenab; those two measures must never be mixed in comparisons.

The printed riverbank-city column includes examples such as Haridwar, Kanpur, Varanasi and Patna on the Ganga; Nashik, Bhadrachalam and Rajamahendravaram on the Godavari; and Mahabaleshwar, Nagarjuna Sagar and Vijayawada on the Krishna, although source and confluence locations must not be mislabelled as riverbank cities.

The world-river box prints the Nile, Amazon and Yangtze as the longest rivers and Amazon, Congo and Mississippi-Missouri as the largest by basin area; rank depends on measurement method and drainage-area definition and requires an authoritative comparative dataset.

pages.heading: Indian drainage-basin area, annual runoff and selected minor rivers

facts.claim: The printed basin-area table ranks the Ganga, Indus, Godavari, Krishna, Brahmaputra, Mahanadi, Narmada and Cauvery by drainage area within India, with international totals supplied for some transboundary systems; all rows must use the same geographic scope.

The table prints 861,404 sq km for the Ganga basin in India, 321,000 for Indus, 313,000 Godavari, 259,000 Krishna, 258,000 Brahmaputra, 142,000 Mahanadi, 99,000 Narmada and 81,155 Cauvery; every value and percentage requires reconciliation with the current official basin atlas.

The printed annual-water table assigns shares to Brahmaputra, Ganga, Godavari, Indus, Mahanadi, Krishna and Narmada and groups the remaining 20.4% under other rivers; these estimates depend on the stated CWC dataset and period.

The page identifies Ganga, Yamuna, Sabarmati and Damodar as heavily polluted rivers in an exam-oriented list; pollution status is time-sensitive and must be tied to a named CPCB assessment rather than treated as a permanent four-river ranking.

Pushkar Lake is a sacred lake in Rajasthan associated with Brahma worship; the printed claim that its excavation began in 1676 must be checked because the lake and pilgrimage tradition are much older than that date.

The Saraswati is described in historical, textual and palaeochannel contexts; claims of present underground flow through Delhi, Hanumangarh, Anupgarh, Barmer and Tanot require clear separation between tradition, hypothesis and verified hydrology.

pages.heading: Genetic classification of rivers and introduction to drainage patterns

facts.claim: Antecedent rivers establish their courses before tectonic uplift and maintain them through incision; Indus, Sutlej and Brahmaputra are standard Himalayan examples, while several additional printed examples require individual verification.

Consequent streams follow the initial regional slope or land-surface gradient; they are not defined by rejuvenation, and Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery and Mahanadi are commonly cited Peninsular examples flowing with the regional easterly slope.

Subsequent streams develop later along zones of weaker rock or structural weakness, commonly at right angles to consequent streams; tributaries such as Chambal, Betwa, Sind, Ken, Damodar and Son need example-by-example verification.
Resequent streams flow in the same general direction as the original consequent drainage but develop at a later stage, often at a lower structural level.
Obsequent streams flow opposite to the original consequent slope and commonly join subsequent streams; they must not be described simply as all tributaries flowing against a main river.

Insequent streams show no strong adjustment to geological structure and may develop irregular courses; headward erosion is a process that can extend drainage but is not by itself the definition of an insequent stream.

Superimposed or epigenetic drainage develops on a former cover surface and retains its course while cutting into an underlying structure; it is distinct from antecedent drainage, although both may cut across structure.

A drainage pattern is the plan-view arrangement of a river and its tributaries, controlled by slope, rock type, geological structure and drainage history; dendritic is the first pattern introduced on this page.

pages.heading: Major drainage patterns

facts.claim: Dendritic drainage resembles branching tree limbs and commonly develops on relatively uniform rock or gently sloping surfaces with limited structural control; a finer feather-like variant is called pinnate.
Trellis drainage develops where strong and weak rock bands alternate, with short tributaries entering a main subsequent valley at near-right angles; folded and cuesta terrain are typical settings.

Rectangular drainage is controlled by joints and faults that produce frequent right-angle bends; angular drainage is similar but follows acute or obtuse fracture intersections rather than predominantly 90-degree turns.

Parallel drainage develops on steep or uniformly sloping elongated terrain where channels run nearly parallel, whereas radial drainage flows outward from a central high such as a dome or volcanic cone.
Annular drainage follows concentric zones of weak rock around a structural dome or basin, producing a ring-like pattern; the printed examples require geological map verification.

The printed diagram depicts dendritic, trellis, radial, sub-dendritic, parallel, sub-parallel, annular, rectangular and pinnate patterns; labels and sketches should be recreated as an accessible visual alongside explanatory text.

pages.heading: Andhra Pradesh drainage overview and Penna profile

facts.claim: Andhra Pradesh generally slopes eastward, so most rivers drain toward the Bay of Bengal; major interstate systems include the Godavari, Krishna, Penna and Tungabhadra, while several shorter rivers rise in the Eastern Ghats and coastal uplands.

The printed Andhra Pradesh drainage map labels major river systems, reservoirs and lakes including Godavari, Krishna, Penna, Vamsadhara, Nagavali, Gundlakamma, Kolleru, Pulicat, Yeleru and Somasila; current district and project labels require map verification.

The Penna rises in the Nandi Hills region of Karnataka, enters Andhra Pradesh and flows through the Rayalaseema and SPSR Nellore region before reaching the Bay of Bengal; the book uses pre-reorganisation district names that must be updated.
The page prints a Penna basin area of about 55,000 sq km, an Andhra Pradesh share of 87% and a total length of 600 km; these values must be checked against an official basin report.
Penna is also known as Pinakini or Pennar, but the etymological statement connecting Pinakini to Shiva's bow should be presented as traditional nomenclature rather than hydrological evidence.

The page lists Jayamangali, Kunderu and Sagileru as left-bank tributaries and Chitravati, Cheyyeru and Papagni as right-bank tributaries of the Penna; the bank designation is repeated in a boxed comparison and must be verified from flow direction.

The page names Nellore, Ranganayaka temple, Jonnawada Kamakshi temple and Gandikota gorge as cultural or physical landmarks associated with the Penna; each location must be separated from the river-course narrative.

pages.heading: Penna tributary profiles and Vamsadhara

facts.claim: Chitravati, Papagni and Cheyyeru are described as right-bank tributaries of the Penna; their Karnataka or Andhra Pradesh origins, district routes and confluences must be updated to current administrative geography.

The Chitravati flows through the Puttaparthi region and joins the Penna in the Gandikota sector; the printed statement about a proposed barrage near Varagudu requires current project-status verification.

Papagni rises in Karnataka and joins the Penna in the Kadapa-region course, while Cheyyeru forms from the Bahuda and Puncha streams and joins the Penna in the Siddavatam region; printed district names require updating.
Jayamangali, Kunderu and Sagileru are left-bank tributaries of the Penna; local place-name and confluence details require official map verification.
Vamsadhara rises in Odisha, flows through Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, and enters the Bay of Bengal near the Kalingapatnam coast; it is an interstate east-flowing river.
The book prints a Vamsadhara length of 226 km, with 130 km in Andhra Pradesh and 96 km in Odisha, and a basin area of 10,830 sq km; all figures require official tribunal or basin-source verification.

The Andhra Pradesh-Odisha dispute concerns use and regulation of Vamsadhara waters, including Gotta Barrage and Neradi-related proposals; project and tribunal status must be dated and neutrally stated.
Srimukhalingam temple and Kalingapatnam are notable cultural and coastal locations associated with the Vamsadhara course in Srikakulam district.

pages.heading: Nagavali and shorter north-coastal Andhra Pradesh rivers

facts.claim: The Nagavali rises in Odisha, flows through Odisha and north-coastal Andhra Pradesh, and enters the Bay of Bengal near the Srikakulam coast; the page prints a total length of 208 km and basin area of 9,510 sq km, requiring official verification.
The page lists Jhanjavati, Suvarnamukhi, Vedavati, Vottigedda, Relligedda, Barha and Satnala among Nagavali tributaries; spellings, bank positions and confluences require basin-map verification.
Jhanjavati is an interstate tributary of the Nagavali with a rubber-dam project near Rajyalakshmipuram; the page's claims about dam rank, inauguration and dimensions require current project records.
Suvarnamukhi or Swarnamukhi, Sarada and Gosthani are distinct east-flowing coastal rivers; their origins, temple or cave associations, and Bay of Bengal outlets must be kept in separate profiles.

Bahuda, Mahendratanaya, Pedda Gedda and Champavati are additional short rivers crossing or draining the Odisha-Andhra coastal belt; printed lengths and administrative routes require current map verification.

The page associates Gosthani with Borra Caves and states that the river later joins the Bay of Bengal near the Visakhapatnam coast; the groundwater-karst connection and exact surface course need careful explanation.

pages.heading: Other Andhra Pradesh coastal rivers and waterfall box

facts.claim: Tandava, Yeleru and Maddigedda are short east-flowing rivers or tributary systems in the north and central Andhra Pradesh region; project names and outlet descriptions require official map verification.

Budameru is a seasonal stream draining toward the Kolleru and Krishna-delta region and is associated with flood risk around Vijayawada; the page's historical diversion statement and 'Vijayawada sorrow' nickname require sourced explanation.

Tammileru, Upputeru, Erra Kaluva and Munneru are hydrologically distinct: Upputeru is the outlet channel connecting Kolleru toward the sea, while the others belong to different drainage or tributary systems.

Gundlakamma rises in the Nallamala region, flows through the Prakasam district area and enters the Bay of Bengal; it is described as the largest among the smaller rivers originating wholly within Andhra Pradesh, a superlative requiring a defined comparison set.
Kalingi and Arani or Korattalaiyar are southern coastal river systems, while the latter is shared with Tamil Nadu; source and outlet locations require current topographic verification.

The waterfall box begins with Talakona, Duduma, Kailasakona, Ubbalamadugu or Tada, Kaigal, Katiki, Tadimada and Kapila Theertham, giving locations, heights or associated streams; every printed cell requires verification.

pages.heading: Andhra Pradesh waterfalls, interstate rivers and cross-state projects

facts.claim: The waterfall list continues with Mallela Theertham, Kailasakona, Ubbalamadugu, Kaigal, Katiki, Tadimada, Nagalapuram and Penchalakona; claims about perennial flow, height, trekking and temple association must be separately verified.
The page states that Andhra Pradesh has about 40 rivers of which 15 are interstate; this count depends on inclusion rules and requires a current state water-resources source.

The interstate-river table lists Bahuda, Mahendratanaya, Pundi Vagu, Vamsadhara and Nagavali with Odisha; Godavari with several states; Krishna with Maharashtra, Telangana and Karnataka; and Penna, Arani, Korattalaiyar, Palar, Ponnaiyar, Budameru, Erra Kaluva and Tammileru with their printed neighbouring-state combinations.

Each interstate classification must be verified because several entries are tributaries or drainage channels rather than independent interstate rivers, and the printed state list may omit or overstate hydrological connections.

The page lists interstate barrages, dams or projects on Vamsadhara, Nagavali, Gosthani, Champavati, Sarada, Yeleru, Godavari, Krishna and Gundlakamma; project name, location, operating status and benefiting states must be verified individually.

pages.heading: Ganga profile, conservation programmes, tributaries and Panch Prayag

facts.claim: The book prints a total Ganga length of about 2,525 km and an Indian basin area of 861,404 sq km, with state-wise lengths; these values must be tied to a single official source and river-segment definition.
The Ganga basin is the largest river basin in India; any claim that it is the fourth largest in the world requires definition and an authoritative comparative dataset.
The Ganga was declared India's National River in 2008; the printed February 2009 date needs correction against the government notification or programme record.
facts.verification_note: Verify the formal declaration date and distinguish it from later authority/programme dates.

facts.claim: Namami Gange is a central integrated conservation mission launched for pollution abatement, conservation and rejuvenation of the Ganga; printed funding periods and amounts are time-sensitive.
The printed 2019 Save Rivers campaign, polluted-stretch categories and example rivers require verification against the relevant pollution-control authority report before scoring.
Important Ganga tributaries must be organised by left bank, right bank and direct headstream relationship rather than memorised as one undifferentiated list.
Panch Prayag comprises Vishnuprayag, Nandaprayag, Karnaprayag, Rudraprayag and Devprayag along the Alaknanda system.
The correct confluences are Vishnuprayag: Dhauliganga-Alaknanda; Nandaprayag: Nandakini-Alaknanda; Karnaprayag: Pindar-Alaknanda; Rudraprayag: Mandakini-Alaknanda; Devprayag: Bhagirathi-Alaknanda.
facts.verification_note: The printed box incorrectly gives Mandakini at Nandaprayag; replace it with Nandakini.

facts.claim: Prayagraj is the confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna, traditionally associated with the invisible Saraswati; it is not one of the five Alaknanda Panch Prayag confluences.
